fields.title: Kromka: ordering supplies for twelve locations
fields.summary: Requirements are short and vague, one person pays, but twelve others will do the work. Decide where to start.
fields.decisionPrompt: Where will you start the first version of the product in eight weeks?
fields.brief/role: You are the first PM at Kromka.
fields.brief/company: Kromka is a fictional chain of twelve coffee shops in one city. The manager at each location orders supplies from five suppliers.
fields.brief/context: The CFO initiated an internal product for ordering supplies: he doesn't see how much is spent by location until the invoices arrive at the end of the month. His requirements list is half a page, all about reporting. Six months ago, the chain already bought a SaaS for procurement, and they abandoned it after two months. You've been given eight weeks to the first version.
fields.brief/objective: Release a version that people will actually start using at all twelve locations, rather than one that looks good on a demo.
fields.brief/constraints: One developer and you, eight weeks. The CFO is the project sponsor and attends every meeting.
fields.brief/task: Decide where you will start and justify the decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When a sponsor asks for visibility, the temptation is to build visibility. But a report only shows what someone entered, and the person entering it has their own job and their own four minutes. The order here is set not by priority, but by dependency: first comes the data stream, then the view of it. And you need to test the product against how the task is solved now — in a messenger, in a notebook, by voice — because that is exactly what it will be compared to.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Half a page, six points:

1. See expenses for each location in real time
2. Convenient report on suppliers
3. Fast approval of large orders
4. Budget limit per location
5. Notifications when exceeded
6. Export for accounting

Not a single point says what is considered 'convenient', 'fast', or 'large'. When asked what a large order is, the CFO replied: 'Well, you know, significant'.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
You visited three locations out of twelve.

The manager looks at the shelves in the morning, sends a voice message to the supplier on WhatsApp, and notes in a notebook what they ordered. It takes four minutes, has worked for years, and errors are rare.

About the previous SaaS: 'There you had to select an item from a thousand-line catalog, specify the quantity, unit of measurement, and confirm. One minute per item. I have twelve of them in an order, and I do this before opening, when the line is already waiting.'

One manager said something worth writing down verbatim: 'It's not hard for me to report. It's hard for me to report and manage to open at the same time.'

None of the three complained about the lack of reports — that's not their problem.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Responsible for keeping locations running. Has never attended a product meeting — says it's a 'finance thing'.

In a hallway conversation, he said: 'If your system causes a location to run out of milk even once, I will shut it down.' Formally, he can: managers report to him, not to finance.

His own metric is the number of hours a location couldn't sell an item due to a lack of supplies. Currently, this is calculated manually once a quarter; last time it was 26 hours across the entire chain.

He was the one who shut down the previous SaaS after orders failed to go through on time at two locations.
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: What can be done in time
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
From the developer:

'Eight weeks is either reporting in full or the order flow in full, but not both.

Order flow: list of items for the location, repeating the last order in one tap, sending to the supplier, marking as received. Five weeks. Repeating the last order is the key thing; without it, it's just the same thousand-line catalog.

Reporting on top of orders: three weeks, but it's pointless until orders are entered into the system.

Budget limits and approvals — another three weeks, and I don't know what is considered a large order.'

The CFO expects a demo in the eighth week.
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Build the order flow so that it takes the manager no more than the current four minutes, and get the data as a side effect. Build reporting on top once orders start being entered.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The order flow is released in the fifth week: list of items for one's location, repeating the last order with one tap, sending, marking as received. Tested at three locations — three and a half minutes compared to four in WhatsApp.
By the eighth week, eleven out of twelve locations are ordering in the system; the twelfth joins two weeks later.
At the demo, the CFO doesn't get the report he asked for — but there is data on all orders for three weeks, from which the report is built. He is unhappy with the format but happy with the content.
The COO comes to the meeting in person for the first time: he now has a downtime figure without manual calculation.
Trade-off: you did not deliver any of the sponsor's six points on time and bet that data is more important than report format.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The CFO pays and decides the fate of the project. Take his six points, clarify the wording, and release reporting by the eighth week.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
By the eighth week, reports, budget limits, and notifications are ready. The demo goes great: the sponsor sees exactly what he asked for.
There is no data in the reports. Orders still go out as voice messages in WhatsApp because entering them in the system takes longer, and managers have no reason to do so.
A month later, the CFO demands that locations be forced to enter orders manually. The COO refuses: his opening times are increasing. The dispute escalates to the owner.
Trade-off: you fulfilled your obligation to the person who pays and built reporting on top of a non-existent data stream.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Return to SaaS, but with training
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The system is already purchased and covers almost everything. Train the managers and implement it properly, and direct the team to other tasks.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Training is conducted at all twelve locations, lasting an hour and a half each. For the first two weeks, orders go through the SaaS.
By the fourth week, eight locations return to WhatsApp. The reason is the same as last time, and it was stated plainly even before starting: one minute per item compared to four minutes for the entire order. Training doesn't change the math.
The COO reminds you that he already shut this down once.
Trade-off: you mistook the rejection of the system for a training problem, even though the cause was measurable and out in the open.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: 'Convenient', 'fast', and 'large' are not verifiable. Spend two weeks turning each point into a verifiable condition and only then plan.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Two weeks are spent on clarification. The result is useful: 'large order' becomes a ruble threshold, 'convenient report' becomes a specific set of dimensions, 'fast' becomes a number.
Six weeks remain for development, with the same fork: order flow or reporting. The choice didn't get any easier, there is just less time.
However, one clarification turns out to be important: when asked about 'real time', the CFO answers that once a day is fine. This removes some of the work.
Trade-off: you removed ambiguity that would have cost dearly later, and spent a quarter of the timeline on it without getting any closer to choosing the order of work.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Requirements were gathered from the loudest person, not from everyone who can stop the project
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: A person with high influence and low interest was not considered until the very end
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: The current way of working is not considered as the main alternative
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: A request was mistaken for a task: the formulation has no verifiable 'so that'
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Scope was cut by importance, not by scenario coherence
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: 'Done' was not defined by a verifiable condition before starting work
